connections.note: The introduction promised that the proofs reach not a vague ‘first cause’ but the God of classical theism. This module cashes that promise for the personal attributes (power, knowledge, goodness, will, love) and for God's ongoing relation to the world.

The Aristotelian proof's purely actual actualizer, sustaining a hierarchical (per se) series here and now, is the basis for omnipotence (all actualizing power), for perfect goodness (goodness as actuality), and for conservation and concurrence. The ladder image recalls that the proofs began from real change.

The Neo-Platonic proof's absolutely simple One grounds incomprehensibility (nothing to analyze into parts), the account of God's knowledge as undivided (prism and dough), and the argument against the existential-inertia thesis (composites need a cause of their unity and being).

The Augustinian proof supplies the realism about universals and the rejection of Platonism that drive the elimination argument for a divine intellect; Feser also points back to chapter 3's forward-route argument for omniscience and its reply to Patrick Grim.

The Thomistic proof's subsistent existence itself grounds the forward route to omnipotence (what exists in the fullest way acts in the fullest way) and the real distinction of creatures from God that rules out pantheism.

The rationalist proof's necessary being and the principle of sufficient reason stand behind proportionate causality and agere sequitur esse; the footnote rejecting the world as the necessary being echoes that chapter.

Part A set out the three tools used throughout this module — proportionate causality, agere sequitur esse, the analogy of being — and derived unity, simplicity, immutability, immateriality, and eternity, plus the fallacy-of-accident reply that is reused here for freedom and love.

Chapter 7 answers general objections to the proofs; this module's picture of God as not ‘a cause among causes’ is key to answering ‘what caused God?’ and the charge that classical theism is a god-of-the-gaps.

The privation account of evil and the courage example here are the foundation for Feser's treatment of the problem of evil in chapter 7; the concurrence account also bears on objections about free will and divine action.

In the capstone, this module supplies the ‘so what’: how the conclusions of five different proofs converge on one personal, omnipotent, omniscient, good God who conserves the world, and how to present that convergence persuasively.

quiz.q: According to Feser, why can't God make a round square?
options: Because his power, though enormous, is finite
Because doing so would conflict with his perfect goodness
Because there is no such thing as a capacity to make a round square; the idea is self-contradictory
Because God freely chose to bind himself to the laws of logic
quiz.explanation: Omnipotence is the power to actualize whatever can be actualized. A round square is not a possible thing, so there is no power there to lack. The last option makes logic a self-imposed rule, which Feser does not claim.

quiz.q: In the ‘backward’ route to omnipotence, Feser combines the dependence of everything on God for existence with which principle?
options: Agere sequitur esse: since acting presupposes existing, what cannot exist on its own cannot act on its own
Proportionate causality: whatever is in the effect is in its cause
The principle that there is no best possible world
The analogy of proper proportionality
quiz.explanation: The key move is that existence is prior to action, so dependence for existence entails dependence for all power. Proportionate causality is the key principle for omniscience and goodness, not this step.

quiz.q: Besides God's immateriality, what further reason does Feser give for denying that creaturely features exist in God as instances?
options: God would then be composed of form and matter
Universals do not really exist
Instances are always imperfect copies
His own instances would need explaining like any others, so he would not be the ultimate cause of things having those features
quiz.explanation: If God merely instantiated redness, his redness would be one more instance needing explanation. The second option contradicts chapter 3's realism about universals, which the argument relies on.

quiz.q: Why does Feser conclude that the forms of all possible things exist in God as concepts in an intellect?
options: Because universals exist only in concrete things, and God is a concrete thing
Because they must be in God somehow (proportionate causality), cannot be there as instances, and there is no Platonic ‘third realm’
Because nominalism shows that universals are just words, and words require a mind
Because God perceives everything and perceptions are mental
quiz.explanation: It is an argument by elimination: instances, intellect, or third realm; not instances, no third realm, so intellect. Nominalism is rejected, not assumed, and God does not perceive.

quiz.q: How does God satisfy the ‘reliable process’ condition of the standard account of knowledge?
options: He observes all events with infallible perception
There is no more reliable way of determining that p is true than being the one who makes p true
He reasons flawlessly from axioms to conclusions
His beliefs are confirmed by the testimony of angels
quiz.explanation: Like an author who knows a character is in the story because he put her there, God knows because he causes. He has no perceptual organs and does not reason step by step.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, doesn't God's knowing all times in a single timeless act imply four-dimensionalism?
options: Because God knows only the present moment
Because four-dimensionalism has been refuted by physics
Because God's knowledge is observational, and observation takes time
Because he knows by being the cause, and knowing timelessly that he causes a temporal world doesn't make that world timeless
quiz.explanation: The inference would work only if God's knowledge were observational. The hunter who knows in an instant that he fired a bullet doesn't make the bullet motionless. Option C gets God's mode of knowing exactly backward.

quiz.q: What is the point of contrasting the crime novel's author with a hypnotist character?
options: Freedom is threatened by a cause acting alongside the agent within the same order, not by the cause of the whole order
Fictional characters lack free will, and so, perhaps, do we
God is more like the hypnotist, but a benevolent one
The author is really just one more character in the story
quiz.explanation: The hypnotist interferes as one character with another; the author interferes with no one because he is not in the story. God's causality is of the author's kind. Option B misreads an illustration of logical compatibility as a claim about fiction.

quiz.q: What are the prism and the lump of dough meant to illustrate?
options: How evil is a privation of good
How God conserves the world in being
How a simple God knows every finite kind by knowing himself as unlimited actuality
How miracles add something new to nature
quiz.explanation: White light contains all colors in a unified way; knowing it perfectly would include knowing every derivable color. So God, knowing himself as pure act, knows every limited way of being actual.

quiz.q: Which of these is a privation, in Feser's sense?
options: A triangle's lacking a fourth side
A tree's lacking wings
A stone's lacking sight
A tree's lacking strong roots
quiz.explanation: A privation is the absence of something a thing's nature calls for. Trees should have strong roots; triangles should not have four sides, trees need no wings, and stones need no sight.

quiz.q: How does Feser answer the objection that pain is a positive bad rather than a privation?
options: Pain is an illusion produced by the brain
Pain is always good, since it warns of danger
What is bad is not pain as such but what it signals or causes — as its warning function, satisfying post-workout aches, and pain asymbolia suggest
Pain is merely the privation of pleasure
quiz.explanation: Feser does not say pain is always good (B), only that it isn't bad without qualification. Its badness lies in the damage it indicates or the lost tranquility it produces.

quiz.q: Why does the objection from a murderer's positive intentions (Calder) fail, according to Feser following Alexander?
options: Because murder is not really bad
Because the privation theory claims only that the badness of an act consists in privation, not that the act has no positive features
Because murderers have no real beliefs or desires
Because intentions are not real mental states
quiz.explanation: The murderer's desire for money may even be good in itself; what is bad is the missing intention to seek money only in ways that respect the innocent. The theory never denied that bad acts contain positive elements.

quiz.q: Why doesn't the principle of proportionate causality imply that evil is in God?
options: Because evil is an absence, not a positive feature, and the principle concerns the positive features of effects
Because the principle applies only to material causes
Because God's causality is equivocal rather than analogical
Because evil has another ultimate cause besides God
quiz.explanation: Making a world with evil means making goods while refraining from making certain other goods, like leaving a triangle unfinished. Feser explicitly rejects restricting the principle to material factors.

quiz.q: What does Feser's courage example show?
options: Some goods cannot exist unless some badness is permitted, so permitting badness is compatible with perfect goodness
God himself lacks the virtue of courage
Courage exists only in heaven
Evil is a positive reality after all
quiz.explanation: Courage requires facing real danger of harm; a world with courage but no danger is as impossible as a round square. The footnote adds that the blessed keep the courage they acquired on earth.

quiz.q: Which example illustrates Barry Miller's notion of a ‘limit case’ (as opposed to a mere limit)?
options: The speed of light, the highest possible speed
A speed of zero, which is not a speed at all, yet is what the ordering of speeds points toward
The largest prime number
The average speed of all moving objects
quiz.explanation: A mere limit (the speed of light) differs from lower speeds only in degree. A limit case differs absolutely, as zero speed is no speed, yet the series points to it. God's will and goodness are limit cases in this sense.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is there nothing internal to God compelling him to create lions rather than unicorns?
options: Because lions are better than unicorns
Because unicorns are impossible
Because nothing in any concept in the divine intellect necessitates that its instances exist or not
Because God lacks the concept of a unicorn
quiz.explanation: Both concepts exist in the divine intellect, and neither contains any necessity of existing or not existing, so before creation either world was equally possible.

quiz.q: What mistake does Feser find in the objection that a simple, purely actual God cannot be free?
options: It wrongly denies divine simplicity
It confuses omnipotence with omniscience
It assumes that God's will is compelled from outside
It commits a fallacy of accident, inferring from the fact that our free choices involve actualizing potentials that free choice as such must
quiz.explanation: The objection assumes simplicity; its error is treating an accompaniment of creaturely freedom as essential to freedom, just as it is an error to think all acting involves changing.

quiz.q: Which two assumptions of the Leibniz/Rowe argument does Feser reject?
options: That God is omnipotent and that he is omniscient
That God exists and that he is good
That one is always obliged to bring about the best one can, and that there is a best possible world
That creatures can be harmed and that God can be harmed
quiz.explanation: No one is wronged if God does not create (not God, not nonexistent trees), and there is no best world since there could always be x + 1 forests.

quiz.q: The perfect diamond that is perfect whether or not it cuts any glass is used to answer which objection?
options: That God cannot suffer with his creatures
That God's knowledge is observational
That miracles violate the laws of nature
Rowe's claim that if there is no best world, there can be no most perfect being
quiz.explanation: God's perfection follows from what he is (pure actuality), not from what he makes, as a diamond's perfection doesn't depend on which glass it cuts.

quiz.q: On Feser's account, what is essential to love?
options: Willing the good of the beloved
Being emotionally affected by the beloved
Needing the beloved
Desiring to possess the beloved
quiz.explanation: Emotions usually accompany our love, but treating them as essential is a fallacy of accident. Tough love and love of enemies show that the will is what makes love real.

quiz.q: Why can't we comprehend God in the strict sense?
options: Because we don't yet have enough empirical data about him
Because strict comprehension works by analyzing things into parts or into genus and specific difference, and God is absolutely simple
Because God deliberately conceals his nature
Because all language about God is metaphorical
quiz.explanation: God is hard to understand precisely because he is simple (partless). Feser insists analogical language is literal, not metaphorical, so option D is a misreading.

quiz.q: What is Feser's response to the thesis of ‘existential inertia’?
options: It contradicts Newtonian physics
It is true of material things but not of immaterial ones
It applies to God rather than to creatures
Its defenders never explain it, and nothing composite of act and potency or of essence and existence could have it
quiz.explanation: Composite, contingent things need a sustaining cause at every moment; merely suggesting existential inertia ignores rather than answers the arguments of earlier chapters.

quiz.q: Someone says: ‘The sun doesn't really melt the ice; God melts it whenever the sun is out.’ Which view is this?
options: Occasionalism
Mere conservationism
Concurrentism
Deism
quiz.explanation: Occasionalism denies creatures any causal efficacy; mere conservationism (and deism) makes creatures act independently of God; concurrentism affirms real secondary causes acting with God's concurrence.

quiz.q: In Freddoso's blue chalk example, what shows that the chalk is a genuine (though secondary) cause?
options: It moves by itself across the board
The effect would be different if red chalk or a pencil were used
It could exist without anyone holding it
It produces the square without the hand
quiz.explanation: A secondary cause is a true cause because it makes a real contribution to the character of the effect, and secondary because nothing happens without the primary cause (your hand).

quiz.q: How do Feser and Oderberg interpret a miracle like the fire's failing to burn Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego?
options: As a breach of the law that fire burns
As evidence that fire's nature was changed permanently
As a suspension: God refrains from conserving or concurring with some of the factors, so the normal effect does not arise
As a preternatural effect produced by angels
quiz.explanation: A breach (fire acting against its nature while all conditions are sustained) is impossible. God simply does not bring about certain things, like a musician omitting notes or a government temporarily revoking a law.

quiz.q: Why does Feser hold that laws of nature are metaphysically necessary (given that the relevant things exist)?
options: Because God decreed them and cannot change his mind
Because they are statistical regularities that have never failed
Because they express the natures of things, so a thing obeying different laws would have a different nature and be a different thing
Because physics has discovered they are mathematically unavoidable
quiz.explanation: Laws are laws of the natures of things: whatever reliably turned into chocolate mousse at 32°F wouldn't be water. The Humean regularity view (B) is exactly what Feser rejects.

shortAnswer.q: Give both of Feser's routes to divine omnipotence, and explain why the paradox of the stone does not refute it.
shortAnswer.model:
**Backward:** everything other than God is composite and contingent and exists at each instant only because God causes it. Since action follows being and existing is presupposed by acting, what cannot exist independently cannot act independently. So all power derives from God and nothing is beyond his power.

**Forward:** God is subsistent existence, existing in the fullest way; to have power is to be able to actualize potential; so, by action follows being, he can act in the fullest way, and nothing could prevent him from actualizing any actualizable potential.

**Stone:** omnipotence covers whatever could exist or occur. A stone's rising can always occur, so God can always cause it; ‘a stone too heavy for God to lift’ is self-contradictory like ‘round square,’ so there is no capacity to lack.
rubric: States the dependence-for-existence premise
Uses agere sequitur esse to extend dependence to action
Gives the forward route from subsistent existence and power as actualizing potential
Explains that contradictions name no possible capacity
Applies this specifically to the stone

shortAnswer.q: Reconstruct Feser's argument that there is an intellect in God.
shortAnswer.model: Everything that exists or could exist depends on God's causal action at every moment. By proportionate causality, whatever is in an effect is in its total cause in some way, so every feature of every possible thing must be in God somehow. Not as instances: God is immaterial, and if he merely instantiated redness his redness would itself need explaining, so he wouldn't be the ultimate cause. Chapter 3 showed universals are real and that, apart from concrete instances, they could exist only as concepts in an intellect or in a Platonic third realm, which does not exist. So they exist in God as concepts: God has intellect. Likewise states of affairs exist in him as propositions.
rubric: Dependence plus proportionate causality
Rules out existence as instances with both reasons
Invokes realism about universals and rejection of Platonism
Draws the conclusion by elimination
Extends to propositions/states of affairs

shortAnswer.q: How does God know the world, according to Feser, and how does this help with (a) four-dimensionalism and (b) free will?
shortAnswer.model:
God knows the world not by observing it but by knowing himself as its cause, in a single timeless act, as an author knows his story by knowing his own intentions. He is not in time, has no senses, and cannot learn.

(a) Four-dimensionalism would follow only if the knowledge were observational. Knowing from outside time that one causes a temporal world does not make the world timeless (the motionless hunter and the moving bullet).

(b) Knowledge as such does not compel (knowing you sit in the next room). And causation by God is like an author's writing a free character, not like a hypnotist character interfering; God is not a cause alongside us, so his causality doesn't rival our freedom.
rubric: Knowledge by causation / self-knowledge, not observation
Grounds this in eternity, incorporeality, immutability
Hunter/bullet point against four-dimensionalism
Knowledge doesn't compel (next room / crystal ball)
Author vs. hypnotist and the analogical point

shortAnswer.q: Explain the privation account of badness and answer two objections to it.
shortAnswer.model:
A thing is good as a specimen to the extent it actualizes what its nature calls for (the ruled triangle, the deep-rooted tree); badness is the absence of such actuality — a privation, the lack of something the nature calls for (a wavy side, weak roots — not a missing fourth side or missing wings). Goodness is primary, badness derivative, as blindness is the lack of sight.

**Evil's reality:** calling blindness a lack doesn't deny it's real; it explains what it is. **Pain:** pain isn't bad without qualification (it warns; post-workout pain can satisfy; asymbolia separates pain from unpleasantness); the badness lies in damage or disturbance. (Also acceptable: murderous intention — the positive desires may be good, the badness is the missing respect for rights; sadism — misdirected desire, a psychological deformity.)
rubric: Goodness as actualizing one's nature, with an example
Badness as privation, distinguished from mere absence
Goodness primary, badness derivative
Correct reply to one objection
Correct reply to a second objection

shortAnswer.q: Why is God perfectly good, and why doesn't this make him the source of evil?
shortAnswer.model: Forward: goodness is actuality and badness unrealized potential; God is pure act with no potential, so he is purely good. Backward: by proportionate causality, all good in the world is in God as its source, so he is all-good. Evil is not in God, because the principle concerns positive features and evil is an absence: making a world with evil is making goods while refraining from others (the unfinished triangle). Refraining is no defect when there is good reason: the lecturer's incomplete triangle serves a larger good, and some goods, like courage, are impossible without real danger.
rubric: Forward route from pure actuality
Backward route from proportionate causality
Evil as absence, so not required in the cause
Unfinished-triangle illustration
Courage (or lecture) example showing permitting badness is compatible with goodness

shortAnswer.q: Why does God have a will, why is it free, and how does Feser answer Leibniz/Rowe?
shortAnswer.model: Natures incline toward their ends: unconsciously (trees), with sensory appetite (dogs), rationally (humans). God, having intellect, has the limit case of rational appetite, and since he grasps all possibles but causes only some, something analogous to willing. It is free: nothing external compels him (everything depends on him) and nothing internal (no concept, lion or unicorn, necessitates its instances). Leibniz/Rowe assume one must do the best one can and that there is a best world; but not creating wrongs no one (God needs nothing; nonexistent trees can't be wronged), and there is no best world (x + 1 forests). Rowe's rejoinder fails because God's perfection comes from what he is, not what he makes (the diamond).
rubric: Grades of appetite and the analogy to God
Limit case and choosing among possibles
No external and no internal compulsion
Both false assumptions identified and rebutted
Diamond reply to Rowe's ‘no most perfect being’

shortAnswer.q: Can an immutable God love? Give Feser's argument.
shortAnswer.model: The objection says love requires being affected, and being affected is change. Feser calls this a fallacy of accident: our love usually involves emotional change, but what is essential to love is willing the good of the beloved. That's why love that is only fluctuating feeling is shallow, while love that keeps willing the other's good (tough love, love of enemies) is serious. Love is chiefly an act of will, which is active, not a passion. God has will, and creating is actualizing, which is willing that things exist with all the goods their natures call for (a tree's roots and photosynthesis). So God loves his creatures, without change.
rubric: States the objection
Identifies the fallacy of accident
Love's essence as willing the good, with supporting examples
Creation as willing existence and good
Conclusion: love without change

shortAnswer.q: In what sense can we comprehend God and in what sense not? Why is this not obscurantism?
shortAnswer.model: Loosely, yes: we understand the arguments; negative knowledge is real knowledge; positive predicates apply literally by analogy — attribution (God primary analogate of power, the sun secondary) and proper proportionality (tree, human, angel, and God each related to their own goodness; God's as the limit case). Strictly, no: full comprehension analyzes things into parts or genus and difference, and God is simple, so the positive content of our concepts thins out. Not obscurantism, because the limitation is derived from the arguments themselves, and physics likewise uses strange concepts (wave-particles, curved space) far from ordinary experience.
rubric: Negative knowledge as real knowledge
Analogy is literal; both types illustrated
Simplicity blocks strict comprehension via analysis
‘Hard to understand because simple’
Physics parallel / mystery as derived result

shortAnswer.q: Compare occasionalism, mere conservationism, and concurrentism, and give Feser's case for concurrentism.
shortAnswer.model: Occasionalism: only God causes (God melts the ice on the occasion of sun). Mere conservationism: God sustains things, but they act independently. Concurrentism: creatures are real but secondary causes acting only with God's concurrence. Against occasionalism: by action follows being, what does nothing is nothing, so only God would exist; but you exist and are not God (you change, doubt, lack power); and it destroys the proofs' starting point (the ladder). Against mere conservationism: what can act independently can exist independently (deism), yet nothing composite can exist without conservation; it too kicks away the ladder. So concurrentism: the blue chalk (you cause the square, the chalk its blueness), the moon and sun, and — for freedom — the father guiding his son's hand.
rubric: Accurate definitions of all three
Both arguments against occasionalism
Both arguments against mere conservationism
Real-and-secondary characterization
At least one of Feser's illustrations used correctly

shortAnswer.q: What is a miracle on Feser's view, why is it not a ‘violation of a law of nature,’ and what role could miracles play?
shortAnswer.model: Laws describe dispositions things have by nature (water freezing at 32°F), which can be blocked or untriggered; and since laws are the laws of natures, they are metaphysically necessary given the things exist, so violations are impossible. A miracle elevates a thing beyond what any created nature can account for — supernatural, not subnatural (defect) or preternatural (angelic) — so only God can cause it, and he doesn't ‘intervene,’ being no cause alongside others. Miracles can add (resurrection) or subtract (the furnace), the latter by God withholding conservation/concurrence: a suspension, not a breach. Their role: a divine seal confirming revelation, making them the bridge between natural and revealed theology and grounding faith in reason.
rubric: Laws as dispositions of natures
Metaphysical necessity and impossibility of violation
Supernatural vs. preternatural vs. subnatural
Additive vs. subtractive; suspension vs. breach
Evidential role / bridge to revealed theology

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser think it is appropriate to call God ‘he’ even though God is sexless?
shortAnswer.model: God is immaterial and not an animal, so not literally male or female. But he has intellect and will, which define personhood, so ‘it’ is wrong. His relation to the world resembles a father's biological role more than a mother's: the father acts, is unchanged, is not physically dependent on mate or child, and is not physically continuous with the child during gestation; God is active in creating, unchanging, independent, and utterly distinct from the world. Maternal imagery would suggest a God changed by or continuous with the world, i.e., panentheism or pantheism.
rubric: States that God is sexless
Personhood rules out ‘it’
Lists the paternal features
Maps them onto God's relation to the world
Explains what maternal imagery would wrongly suggest

flashcards.front: Two routes Feser uses for most divine attributes
flashcards.back: Backward, from the world as effect (dependence, proportionate causality) and forward, from God's nature as pure act / subsistent existence (agere sequitur esse).

flashcards.front: Why dependence for existence implies dependence for action
flashcards.back: Agere sequitur esse: acting presupposes existing, so what has no independent capacity to exist can have no independent capacity to act.

flashcards.front: Why ‘God can't make a round square’ is no limit on omnipotence
flashcards.back: There is no capacity to make a round square; the description is self-contradictory and names nothing.

flashcards.front: Paradox of the stone: Feser's resolution
flashcards.back: A stone's rising can always occur, so God can always cause it; ‘a stone too heavy for God to lift’ is as contradictory as a round square.

flashcards.front: Two reasons creaturely features aren't in God as instances
flashcards.back: (1) God is immaterial; (2) if he merely instantiated them, his instances would need explaining too, so he wouldn't be the ultimate cause.

flashcards.front: The elimination argument for divine intellect
flashcards.back: Features must be in God somehow; not as instances; universals exist only in instances, in an intellect, or in a Platonic realm; no Platonic realm, so in an intellect.
A proposition (that the cat is on the mat) is the intellect's correlate of a state of affairs (the cat's being on the mat), as a concept is of a universal.

flashcards.front: Standard account of knowledge, and how God meets it
flashcards.back: Believe p, p true, via reliable process. God thinks p; p is true because he causes it; making p true is the most reliable way to ‘find out.’
Not by observation or learning but by knowing himself as its cause, in one timeless act — like an author knowing his story.
Knowing in an instant that one fired a bullet doesn't make the bullet motionless; so timeless knowledge of a temporal world doesn't make the world timeless (against four-dimensionalism).
Knowing doesn't compel: knowing you sit in the next room (now or tomorrow, via promise or crystal ball) doesn't make your sitting unfree.
The author of a crime novel doesn't make the murderer unfree; a hypnotist character would. God is the author — not a cause alongside us.
White light and uncut dough contain colors and shapes in unified form; knowing pure actuality perfectly includes knowing every limited way of being actual.
The degree to which a thing actualizes the potentials its nature directs it toward — objective, as with triangles and trees.
The special case of goodness for free rational creatures who choose to promote or frustrate the realization of potentials they need to flourish.
Privation: lacking what one's nature calls for (weak roots in a tree). Mere absence: lacking what it doesn't (a tree without wings).

flashcards.front: Reply: ‘Privation theory denies evil is real’
flashcards.back: Blindness is the absence of sight and is perfectly real; explaining evil as privation explains its reality, not away.
Pain isn't bad unqualifiedly (it warns; post-workout pain satisfies; pain asymbolia); the badness is the damage or disturbance associated with it.

flashcards.front: Reply to Calder's murder objection (via Alexander)
flashcards.back: Bad acts contain positive features; only their badness is privative — e.g., the missing intention to seek money only by just means.

flashcards.front: Why proportionate causality doesn't put evil in God
flashcards.back: The principle concerns positive features; evil is an absence — goods God refrained from making (the unfinished triangle).
Courage requires real danger of harm; God can't make courage without danger any more than a round square. Some goods require permitting badness.
Natural inclination (tree, unconscious); sensory appetite (dog, conscious); rational appetite or will (human, conceptual).
What a series points to but differs from absolutely — zero speed is not a slowest speed but no speed. God's will and goodness are limit cases.
Nothing external compels him (all depends on him); nothing internal does (no concept, lion or unicorn, necessitates its instances).
Fallacy of accident: our free choices actualize potentials, but freedom as such needn't. Davies: read divine freedom as ‘not compelled.’
That one must always do the best one can (no one is wronged by not being created) and that there is a best world (always x + 1 forests).
A perfect diamond is perfect whatever glass it cuts, or none; God's perfection comes from what he is, not what he makes (against Rowe).

flashcards.front: Essence of love, and why God loves creatures
flashcards.back: Love is willing the good of the beloved — active will, not passive emotion (hence tough love, love of enemies). To create is to will that things exist with all the goods their natures call for.

flashcards.front: Loose vs. strict comprehension of God
flashcards.back: Loose: real negative and literal analogical knowledge. Strict: impossible, since God is simple and can't be analyzed into parts or genus and difference.
Nothing distinct from God could exist an instant without his sustaining it; creation happens at every moment.
Never explained; and impossible for anything composite of act and potency or of essence and existence.
(1) What does nothing is nothing, so only God would exist — but you exist and aren't God. (2) It undermines the proofs' starting points (the ladder).
(1) What could act independently could exist independently — deism — yet nothing composite can. (2) It too blasts away the ladder.
Secondary causes are real (they contribute) and secondary (inert without God). Blue chalk: you cause the square, the chalk its blueness.
The child can resist or cooperate, contributing really, but no letter A appears without the father — how concurrence leaves freedom intact.
Supernatural: beyond any created nature (only God). Preternatural: extraordinary but within created powers (angels). Subnatural: defects.
To interfere you must be alongside what you interfere with; God causes everything and is alongside nothing. You can't intervene in what you're doing yourself.
Breach: law in force but unenforced. Suspension: law temporarily revoked. Subtractive miracles (the furnace) are God withholding conservation or concurrence.
Only God can work miracles, so they can certify a revelation (‘seal of approval’), grounding faith — believing because God revealed — in reason.
Personal (intellect and will), and relation to the world like a father's: active, unchanged, independent, distinct. Maternal imagery suggests pantheism or panentheism.

teachBack:
**The challenge:** Explain to a thoughtful friend who is *not* religious, in about eight minutes, how Feser gets from “a purely actual First Cause” to “an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good, free, loving God who is not a cause among causes.”

**Constraints:**
- Use no technical Latin except, once, “action follows being,” and explain it in plain words.
- You must use exactly three analogies: the author of a novel (for knowledge and freedom), the unfinished triangle (for goodness and evil), and the blue chalk or the jazz musician (for concurrence or miracles). For each, say out loud where the analogy breaks.
- You must state and answer, in your own words, at least three objections: the stone, foreknowledge vs. free will, and ‘an unchanging God can't love.’
- End by explaining why God is knowable but not fully comprehensible, without using the word ‘mystery’ as a conversation-stopper.

**Check yourself:**
1. Did you derive each attribute from something already established, rather than just asserting it? Could you name the principle used at each step (dependence, action follows being, proportionate causality)?
2. Did you avoid saying God ‘foresees,’ ‘intervenes,’ or ‘breaks laws’?
3. Did you keep both halves of concurrence (creatures really cause; they cause only with God)?
4. Did you distinguish privation from mere absence with an example?
5. Could your friend repeat the author-vs-hypnotist point back to you? Ask them to. If they can't, re-teach that piece first — it carries most of the module.
videoPrompt: Audience: curious, intelligent adults with no philosophy background, some skeptical. Goal: show how, once the five proofs establish a purely actual First Cause that sustains everything, Feser derives God's other attributes and his relationship to the world. Emphasize, in order: (1) omnipotence — all power is borrowed from the source of existence; the stone paradox dissolves because contradictions aren't things; (2) omniscience — God knows like an author, by causing, not by watching; author vs. hypnotist for free will; (3) goodness as actuality and evil as privation, using the triangle and tree examples and the courage point; (4) God's free will, no best possible world, and love as willing good rather than feeling; (5) knowable but not fully comprehensible because simple; (6) concurrence — the blue chalk — versus occasionalism and deism; (7) miracles as elevation or suspension, never violation, with the jazz musician. Correct the misconceptions that God is a super-person, that he ‘foresees,’ and that miracles break laws. Tone: clear, warm, intellectually serious, never preachy.
